title: Vision-guided navigation on a microcontroller robot
summary: A single-camera mobile robot that tracks moving targets, judges obstacle distance from monocular geometry, and explores an unknown grid - all reasoning happening on the microcontroller itself, no external computer or localization.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Give a small wheeled robot everything it needs to navigate using nothing but a single onboard camera and a microcontroller - no GPS, no external localization, no offboard compute. That splits into three connected problems.
list: Track a moving visual target in closed loop
Judge how far away an obstacle is from a single 2D image, with no depth sensor
Build up a map of an unknown space from nothing but local visual landmarks

sections.heading: Approach
list: A PID controller keeps the pan servo locked onto a coloured blob, tuned by physically running the robot against a monitor playing a moving target at swept frequencies (0.03-2.8 Hz) and swept gains, logging error and angle at every step

Obstacle distance comes from a single-camera trick: calibrate once against a reference object of known real-world size, then convert an obstacle's apparent size and position into a real distance and bearing using the law of cosines, accounting for the blind zone directly beneath the camera's field of view
The exploration and mapping logic builds an internal grid incrementally from blob-based landmarks. It went through six full rewrites, and is the part I iterated on hardest

sections.heading: Result
body: Getting the tracking loop running at all was harder than tuning it well. The debugging session log records what that actually took.
list: 28 run attempts, of which only 17 reached a working calibration
66 outright calibration failures - mostly the pan servo's required sweep being defeated by how the robot was physically angled at the screen

body: Going back to the logged sweep data, the responsiveness/smoothness trade-off is clearly there: pushing the proportional gain from 0.5 to 1.2 cut tracking error by 54%, but nearly tripled the rate at which the servo reversed direction. A more responsive loop, at a direct and measurable cost.

sections.heading: What the rewrites recorded
body: Every rewrite of the mapping code was saved as its own file rather than committed to git, so the failures are all still there to read.
list: One version's edge detection never fired at all: the blob detector returns an empty list rather than None, and the code checked for the wrong one
A turn-selection gain was accidentally set roughly 90 times too high, and shipped for two full versions before being caught
A sorting bug made the robot execute its right-hand turns in the wrong order
The reverse manoeuvre carries a comment saying it "DEFINITELY needs tuning" in the very first version. The identical comment is still there, unresolved, in the final one
